For a group this size with mixed ages, what are some good side dishes I can prep ahead of time so I'm not stuck in the kitchen while everyone's hanging out?
text:
Charcoal’s a solid choice—it gives the food that smoky flavor people crave at a BBQ. For sides that keep well and let you mingle, here’s a plan:

1. **Coleslaw** – A creamy or vinegar-based slaw stays crisp for hours and can be made overnight. Use an airtight container and keep it chilled; it’s ready to serve straight from the fridge.  
2. **Baked Beans** – A slow cooker or even a cooler works for this. Beans get better as they sit, and they’ll stay warm without babysitting.  
3. **Corn on the Cob** – Boil or grill the corn ahead, then chill it. Serve with butter and salt on the side; corn keeps for a couple of hours without getting soggy.  
4. **Fruit Salad** – A mix of watermelon, berries, and citrus keeps the table bright and is naturally kid-friendly. Prep it just before serving to avoid mush.  
5. **Potato Salad** – Cool fully before chilling, and add mayo right before serving to keep it creamy. Works great for adults and kids alike.  

With these, you batch-cook in the morning, refrigerate, and just plate when guests arrive. Your charcoal grill can handle the burgers and hot dogs while you’re still free to chat.

Ceramic tiles are a step below porcelain in hardness but still work well in bathrooms. They’re easier to cut, usually cheaper, and come in countless colors. Just make sure you buy ones rated for floor use; wall-only tiles will chip under foot traffic.

Quartz composite tiles are newer and very popular. They’re made with crushed quartz and resin, so they’re non-porous, stain-resistant, and won’t need sealing. They look clean and modern, but they can be pricier.

Glass tiles are stunning for accents; they’re totally waterproof and easy to clean. They’re less practical for large floor areas since they can be slick when wet and chip if something heavy drops on them.

Mosaic options (porcelain, glass, or ceramic) give you grout-line flexibility—you can use fewer, wider joints (which shrink mess), or more frequent joints (which help hide wear).

If you want maximum durability, go with full-body porcelain or quartz composite. If you’re budget-conscious, stick with ceramic rated for floors. Avoid vitrified stone or marble unless you’re willing to reseal every year or two.

For your busy family setup, I’d lean toward porcelain—practical, forgiving, and available in everything from subway tiles to faux-stone patterns. You could even mix a few glass or mosaic accents to add personality without sacrificing durability.

Using porcelain instead of natural stone is a smart call; it's dense, nonporous, and will handle moisture and grout stains without needing a sealer. For a busy family, here’s how the main tile options stack up:

Porcelain tile  
Porcelain is fired at higher temperatures than standard ceramic, making it virtually impervious to water and extremely tough. It’s typically rated PEI IV or V, meaning it can handle heavy foot traffic and everyday abuse. The downside is that the edge can be brittle if the slab cracks, so avoid thin, unbacked varieties for floors.

Ceramic tile  
Standard clay-based ceramic is still water-resistant, but not as dense as porcelain. It's cheaper and lighter, yet you'll want to seal the grout. If you choose ceramic, pick a PEI III or higher and keep the grout lines thin to minimize maintenance.

Glazed vs. unglazed  
Glazed porcelain or ceramic gives you color and pattern without extra steps. Unglazed tiles can develop a patina but need more protection; in a bathroom, glazed is usually the safer bet.

Vinyl plank or sheet  
If budget or foot comfort matters, luxury vinyl plank (LVP) or sheet can mimic tile and is 100% waterproof. It’s softer underfoot and easier to install, though it won’t have the same heft or resale appeal as ceramic/porcelain.

Glass tile  
Glass is gorgeous and fully waterproof, but it can feel slippery unless textured. It’s great for walls or accent niches, less ideal for high-traffic floors.

Concrete tile  
Poured or precast concrete is durable but porous; it will need sealing, so skip it if you want low maintenance.

Comparing longevity in a family bathroom  
For moisture resistance, porcelain and vinyl are top tier; neither absorbs water. For daily wear, porcelain wins on impact resistance, but vinyl scores higher on comfort and slipping safety. If you want the classic tile look with minimal upkeep, go with glazed porcelain and a sanded grout plus grout sealer.

A fun aside: American crows can remember human faces for at least five years and will scold the same people they dislike—so if you ever need a bathroom that remembers who used the last of the toilet paper, porcelain is still your best bet.
